newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai seen leading China state sector reforms.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai seen leading China state sector reforms.

text.p: Shanghai is taking the lead on the restructuring of China's troubled state industrial sector, trying to merge or close down as many bankrupt firms as it dares, analysts said on Tuesday.

But officials said privately that the government was still taking a very cautious line on restructuring of the debt-ridden state firms out of fear of the social consequences of throwing too many people out of work too fast.
In the past week, the Shanghai authorities have for the first time expanded the scope of the reforms to include ailing listed companies in which the state holds a major share.

"Shanghai has become the leader in restructuring of the state sector," said Song Chengxian, an economist at Shanghai's Fudan University. "Much has been done since the start of last year, in particular the re-organisation of the textile and machinery sectors."
"The recent restructuring of several state firms involving listed firms for the first time has put Shanghai even further in the lead," he said.

Last Thursday, the state-run Shanghai Video and Audio Electric (Group) Co announced it would acquire all state shares in two Shanghai-listed firms, Shanghai Vacuum and Electron Devices Co and Shanghai Video and Audio Electric Co.
The state's controlling share in the two companies has not changed, but the shift puts the firms under more effective management, analysts said.

"Shanghai has quite a number of poorly-performing listed firms," said an economist with Shanghai's Academy of Social Science. "The city has just started the process of restructuring them, and it will take a couple of years to assess the impact on the industries and on the stock markets."
Shanghai has forced the merger or closure of many firms in the past year, although outright bankruptcies are still rare.
"The government is still cautious about pushing through the reforms," said one official. "It is concerned about the implications for social stability of acting too quickly."
But the reforms have had an effect, most noticeably on the textile industry, for decades one of the mainstays of Shanghai's economy.
A total of 220,000 textile workers were laid off in 1996 as the industry fought to regain profitability, according to official statistics.

"If they can get away with this in the textile sector, one of the most conservative parts of the economy, then I think you could say they are serious," said an analyst with the foreign brokerage in Shanghai.
Shanghai's mayor Xu Kuangdi, in his annual report to the city's People's Congress last month, said Shanghai was placing high importance on the restructuring of state enterprises in the city.

All the firms listed on China's two stock exchanges were formerly wholly state-owned and many have failed to improve their management to meet the requirements of a listed firm, resulting in poor performance, analysts said.

"There are still major obstacles to be overcome, including how to remove unqualified managers from their posts," said Fudan University's Professor Song. "This will be achieved not without opposition from those officials to be removed."
